text:
Moth and Gravel, Field Note 9, A
Place to Stand. An AI narrated

edition of the published note. A
pony stands beside a block. Turn

the island a little and its feet
disappear into the ground.

Nothing has moved except the
view.

A small island asks for a
particular kind of trust. The

player looks, chooses a place,
and tries something there. The

picture needs to keep its
account of where things are,

even as the camera wanders. The
ground has to keep its word. Sky

Stack Builders renderer
experiments begin with that

agreement. The game keeps a
shared camera for drawing and

choosing a place. But a common
view does not give every drawn

detail a dependable position
within it. The broad face of a

block is one thing. A bevel, a
patch of soil, and the edge of a

pony's foot each need to belong
somewhere too. If their depth is

guessed badly, a small detail
can cover something that ought

to be in front of it. Let the
pony show through everything and

the feet return. So does a
different problem. A raised

block can no longer hide the
pony when it should. The useful

answer has to preserve both
relationships. Feet meet the

ground. A wall can still stand
in the way.

Take a little away and look
again.

During an earlier investigation,
one fixed camera view lost part

of the pony's body and much of
its contact with the ground. A

second version left out some
terrain details. All the sampled

parts of the pony returned. That
comparison gave the work a place

to look. Something among the
omitted details deserved closer

attention. It also left the
island incomplete. The patches

and edges that make a place feel
particular were part of the

picture we wanted to keep. An
earlier investigation into

views. Recorded sample counts
from one camera position. This

schematic is not a game capture
or a statement of the renderer's

current condition. Open the
full-size diagram.

Keep the small things. A patch
of soil deserves an account of

where it belongs, just as the
large block beneath it does. The

repair has to let both remain in
the picture. There is a design

question underneath the drawing
work. Which small agreements

make a strange place feel
dependable? A player may never

notice a correctly hidden hoof.
They notice when a turn of the

camera makes the island
contradict itself. That

interruption can reach beyond
the pony. Is this a place I can

build? Will the block I choose
be the one I meant? Turn the

island again. The next player
study would keep the whole scene

present. Turn the camera, put a
raised block in front of the

pony, try a ramp. Ask someone to
choose a place beside it, then

look from another side. Watch
where they hesitate and what

they believe is touching the
ground. A rendering test can

check sampled pixels. The person
can tell us whether the place

still makes sense. The island
has room for pastel weather and

improbable creatures. Its ground
should be something they can

stand on. Study scope, source
reading. An earlier view. This

study reads an earlier renderer
investigation and its recorded

native test results. The
comparison describes one

historical camera fixture and an
intentionally incomplete

diagnostic. It does not describe
the current renderer's test

status. The cover is editorial
artwork and the comparison is a

schematic of recorded counts. No
new game capture, player

observation, or performance
measurement was made for this

note. The proposed player study
remains to be done. You have

been listening to Moth and
Gravel Field Notes. The written
edition is at mothandgravel.com.
